chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Ismail ibn Abdul Aziz, from his father, from Abu Baseer who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man from our companions who had eight hundred dirhams, and he was a glass polisher, and he had many dependants. Is it permissible for him to take from the Zakat? He (peace be upon him) said: 'O Abu Muhammad, does he profit from his dirhams what would provide for his dependants and there is an excess?' I said, 'Yes'. He (peace be upon him) said: 'How much is the excess?' I said, 'I do not know'. He (peace be upon him) said: 'If the excess upon the provision is the amount of half the provision, then he should not take the Zakat; and if it is less than half the provision, he takes the Zakat.'

I said, 'So, is Zakat imposed upon his wealth that he must pay?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes'. I said, 'What should he do?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'He should expand upon his dependants with it in their food, drink, and clothing; and if something remains from it, he can give it to others; and whatever he takes from the Zakat, he dedicates it to his dependants until he brings them up to the level of the people.'

key_terms.خَفَّاف: Glass polisher (a specific trade mentioned to illustrate modest means)
key_terms.عِيَال: Dependants (family members supported by the head of household)
key_terms.يُلْحِقَهُمْ بِالنَّاسِ: To bring them up to the level of the people (financially)

ai.seo_question: When is a person with some wealth allowed to receive Zakat according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a nuanced criterion for Zakat eligibility based on net disposable wealth rather than gross assets, distinguishing between those who are merely 'light-fingered' (khaffaf) and those truly in need. The Imam clarifies that such individuals remain liable for Zakat, which they should prioritize for their family's sustenance, thereby preventing the depletion of their capital while they strive to achieve financial parity with the general populace. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on self-sufficiency and the strategic use of Zakat as a temporary bridge to economic stability rather than a permanent subsidy.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Bakr Bin Salih, from Al Hassan Bin Ali, from Ismail Bin Abdul Aziz, from his father, from Abu Baseer who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullahasws about a man from our companions for whom were eight hundred Dirhams and he is a man who is a glass polisher, and for him there are a lot of dependants. Is it for him that he takes from the Zakāt?’ So heasws said: ‘O Abu Muhammad! Does he profit regarding his Dirhams what would provide his dependants with and there would be excess?’ I said, ‘Yes’. Heasws said: ‘How much is the excess?’ I said, ‘I don’t know’. Heasws said: ‘If it was so that the excess upon the provision was of a measurement of half the provision, so he cannot take from the Zakāt; but if it was less than half the provision, he can take from the Zakāt’.

I said, ‘So, would Zakāt be Imposed upon his wealth?’ Heasws said: ‘Yes’. I said, ‘How should he deal with it?’ Heasws said: ‘He can expand upon his dependants with it in their foods and their drinks, and their clothing; and if there was to remain something from it, he can give it to others; and whatever he takes from the Zakāt, he can dedicate it upon his dependants until he makes them catch up with the people (financially)’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Bakr ibn Salih from al-Hassan ibn Ali from ’Isma‘il ibn ‘Abd al-‘Aziz from his father from abu Basir who has said the following:

“I once asked abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a certain person of our people who has eight hundred dirham, works with pumice, and has a large family to feed, if he can receive Zakat. He (the Imam) asked, ‘O abu Muhammad, can he earn with his dirham the expenses of his family with a certain amount of saving?’ I replied, ‘Yes, he does.’ He (the Imam) then asked, ‘How much does he save?’ I replied, ‘I do not know.’ He (the Imam) said, ‘If his saving amounts to half of his expenses, he cannot receive Zakat, but if it is less than half of his expenses, it is lawful for him to receive Zakat.’

I then asked, ‘Is there any Zakat on his assets?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, there is Zakat on his assets.’ I then asked, ‘How will he deal with it?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘With that he meets his expenses for his family, for their food, drink and clothes, and if anything remains he can give to others and what he receives from Zakat is to raise the standard of the living of his family.’”
